prompt:
A curve $C$ is defined by the parametric equations $x(t)=t^2-2t$ and $y(t)=t^3-12t$.

**(a)** Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ in terms of $t$, and find its value at $t=3$.

**(b)** The curve has a vertical tangent line at one point. Find the point, and write an equation of that tangent line.

**(c)** Find $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ at $t=3$. Is the curve concave up or concave down there? Give a reason.

rubric.description: (b) Checks $\frac{dy}{dt}=-9\ne0$ at $t=1$ and finds the point $(-1,-11)$

sampleResponse:
(a) $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3t^2-12}{2t-2}$; at $t=3$ this is $\frac{15}{4}$.
(b) $\frac{dx}{dt}=0$ when $t=1$, and $\frac{dy}{dt}=3-12=-9\ne0$. The point is $(x(1),y(1))=(-1,-11)$ and the vertical tangent line is $x=-1$.
(c) $\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=\frac{6t(2t-2)-2(3t^2-12)}{(2t-2)^2}=\frac{6t^2-12t+24}{(2t-2)^2}$. Dividing by $\frac{dx}{dt}=2t-2$: $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{6t^2-12t+24}{(2t-2)^3}$. At $t=3$: $\frac{42}{64}=\frac{21}{32}>0$, so the curve is concave up.

prompt:
A particle moves in the $xy$-plane with velocity vector $\vec v(t)=\langle t^2-4,\,2t\rangle$ for $t\ge0$. At time $t=0$ the particle is at the point $(0,3)$.

**(a)** Find the acceleration vector and the speed of the particle at $t=1$.

**(b)** Is the speed of the particle increasing or decreasing at $t=1$? Give a reason for your answer.

**(c)** Find the position of the particle at $t=3$.

**(d)** At what time $t>0$ is the particle moving straight up or straight down?

rubric.description: (b) Decreasing, because the dot product is negative
(c) Integrates each component of the velocity with a constant of integration (or uses the limits 0 to 3)

sampleResponse:
(a) $\vec a(t)=\vec v\,'(t)=\langle2t,2\rangle$, so $\vec a(1)=\langle2,2\rangle$. $\vec v(1)=\langle-3,2\rangle$, so the speed is $\sqrt{9+4}=\sqrt{13}$.
(b) $\vec v(1)\cdot\vec a(1)=-6+4=-2<0$, so the speed is decreasing.
(c) $x(3)=0+\int_0^3\left(t^2-4\right)dt=9-12=-3$ and $y(3)=3+\int_0^32t\,dt=3+9=12$. The position is $(-3,12)$.
(d) The particle moves vertically when $x'(t)=0$ and $y'(t)\ne0$: $t^2-4=0$ gives $t=2$ (for $t>0$), and $y'(2)=4\ne0$.

prompt:
The graphs of the polar curves $r=2\cos\theta$ and $r=1$ are both circles. Let $R$ be the region that lies inside the graph of $r=2\cos\theta$ and outside the graph of $r=1$.

**(a)** Find the two values of $\theta$, with $-\frac\pi2<\theta<\frac\pi2$, at which the graphs intersect.

**(b)** Write an integral expression for the area of $R$, and find the area.

**(c)** Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ for the curve $r=2\cos\theta$ at $\theta=\dfrac\pi3$.

rubric.description: (b) Integrand $\frac12\left(4\cos^2\theta-1\right)$ (outer radius squared minus inner radius squared)
(b) Limits $-\frac\pi3$ to $\frac\pi3$ (or twice the integral from 0 to $\frac\pi3$)

sampleResponse:
(a) $2\cos\theta=1$ gives $\cos\theta=\frac12$, so $\theta=\pm\frac\pi3$.
(b) $A=\frac12\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3}\left(4\cos^2\theta-1\right)d\theta=\frac12\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3}\left(1+2\cos2\theta\right)d\theta=\frac12\left[\theta+\sin2\theta\right]_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3}=\frac12\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}+\sqrt3\right)=\frac\pi3+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
(c) With $r=2\cos\theta$ and $r'=-2\sin\theta$: $\frac{dy}{d\theta}=-2\sin^2\theta+2\cos^2\theta=2\cos2\theta$ and $\frac{dx}{d\theta}=-2\sin\theta\cos\theta-2\cos\theta\sin\theta=-2\sin2\theta$. At $\theta=\frac\pi3$: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2\cos\frac{2\pi}3}{-2\sin\frac{2\pi}3}=\frac{-1}{-\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}$.

prompt:
Consider the polar curve $r=3-2\cos\theta$ for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.

**(a)** Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at $\theta=\dfrac\pi2$.

**(b)** For what values of $\theta$ in $(0,2\pi)$ is the distance from the curve to the origin increasing? Justify your answer.

**(c)** Find the average value of $r$ for $0\le\theta\le\pi$.

**(d)** Find the area enclosed by the curve.
sampleResponse:
(a) At $\theta=\frac\pi2$: $r=3$, $r'=2\sin\theta=2$. $\frac{dy}{d\theta}=2\cdot1+3\cdot0=2$ and $\frac{dx}{d\theta}=2\cdot0-3\cdot1=-3$, so $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac23$.
(b) The distance from the origin is $|r|=r$ (since $r\ge1>0$), and $\frac{dr}{d\theta}=2\sin\theta>0$ for $0<\theta<\pi$. So the distance is increasing on $(0,\pi)$.
(c) $\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi(3-2\cos\theta)\,d\theta=\frac1\pi\left[3\theta-2\sin\theta\right]_0^\pi=3$.
(d) $A=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}\left(9-12\cos\theta+4\cos^2\theta\right)d\theta=\frac12\left(18\pi-0+4\pi\right)=11\pi$.

prompt:
A particle moves along a curve in the plane with position $\left(x(t),y(t)\right)=\left(t+2\sin t,\;2\cos t\right)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$.

**(a)** Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at $t=\dfrac\pi3$.

**(b)** Find all values of $t$ in $(0,2\pi)$ at which the particle's path has a vertical tangent line.

**(c)** A graphing calculator may be used. Write an integral expression for the total distance the particle travels from $t=0$ to $t=2\pi$, and find its value.

rubric.description: (c) Evaluates the integral with the calculator

sampleResponse:
(a) At $t=\frac\pi3$: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2\sin\frac\pi3}{1+2\cos\frac\pi3}=\frac{-\sqrt3}{2}$.
(b) $\frac{dx}{dt}=1+2\cos t=0$ when $\cos t=-\frac12$, so $t=\frac{2\pi}{3}$ or $t=\frac{4\pi}{3}$. At both, $\frac{dy}{dt}=-2\sin t=\mp\sqrt3\ne0$.
(c) Distance $=\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{(1+2\cos t)^2+4\sin^2t}\,dt=\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{5+4\cos t}\,dt\approx13.365$.
